examples.title: Power laws in the doctoral-advisor network
examples.description: Wikidata's 408,000 doctoral supervisions (P184): students per advisor are heavy-tailed (7 advisors with 100+ students, where a same-mean geometric expects 10⁻¹⁰), advisors per student are not. Fitting a power law the right way (Clauset, Shalizi & Newman): CCDF instead of histogram, maximum-likelihood α, x_min by KS distance, Vuong's likelihood-ratio test against an exponential. Caveats: Wikidata coverage bias; lognormal not fitted.

examples.title: Air quality in eight cities
examples.description: Open-Meteo's CAMS air-quality model for eight cities: hourly fine particles (PM2.5) for the past three days and the next two, against the WHO 24-hour guideline (15 µg/m³), and daily means of PM2.5, PM10, NO₂ and ozone. Statistics: the guideline is a 99th percentile (no more than 3–4 days a year above it), so the second graph shows each city's distribution of hours as quantiles and counts the days whose mean exceeds 15. Modelled values, not station measurements; five days are a small sample of a year.

examples.title: Alpha decay: tunnelling explains 40 decades of half-life
examples.description: IAEA's chart of nuclides: every ground state, the valley of stability, and the α emitters. Physics idea: Gamow's quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier, computed from Z, A and Q alone, puts 142 even–even emitters spanning 42 decades of half-life on one line (slope 0.99, scatter 0.4 dex). Caveats: no preformation or centrifugal barrier; odd nuclei are hindered.

examples.title: How unique is an API? A study of the Explore catalog
examples.description: Recomputes Explore's uniqueness score (TF-IDF distinctness × field rarity) from the public catalog: rarity drives the ranking more than the text, the real near-copies are vendor product lines, and per-country copies (energy) are a small effect. Sensitivity to k and to place names, a similarity network, and a study with Welch tests.

examples.title: REST API workbench
examples.description: Developing against a REST API: call endpoints, join their answers and check the shape of the data: which fields every record has, which users and posts match in a full join, and the distribution of body lengths with its quantiles before averaging it. Uses JSONPlaceholder as a stand-in (a fixture: every user has exactly 10 posts); point the datasource at http://localhost:<port> and Seebra calls your local API straight from the browser.

examples.title: Ashby chart: why aircraft are aluminium, CFRP and spruce
examples.description: Young's modulus against density for 438 materials on Wikidata, and the performance indices E/ρ, E^½/ρ, E^⅓/ρ: steel, aluminium and titanium tie as rods, but an aluminium panel weighs half a steel one and spruce a sixth.

examples.title: Beetle species and effort
examples.description: Beetle records in GBIF from three Swedish provinces in 2024, counted per species. Statistics idea: a species count depends on effort: rarefaction gives the species expected in n random records so provinces compare at equal effort, and Chao1 estimates the unseen from species seen once and twice. Caveats: GBIF records are not a random sample, provinces differ in size and habitat, and Chao1 is a lower bound.

examples.title: Benford's law in country statistics
examples.description: Population, land area, GDP and CO₂ emissions of every country from the World Bank, and the first significant digit of each. Statistics idea: Benford's law: quantities spanning several orders of magnitude start with 1 about 30% of the time and with 9 under 5% (log10(1 + 1/d)); a chi-square test and the mean absolute deviation say how close each comes. Caveats: ~215 countries is a small sample for a digit test, values are each country's latest year, and conformity is not proof of honest numbers.

examples.title: How bridges wear out
examples.description: US National Bridge Inventory (FHWA, 2025): condition ratings by age, material and reconstruction. The poor share doubles every ~7 years until 45, then repairs bend the curve; ageing alone takes 41,319 poor bridges to ~56,000 by 2035.

examples.title: The C-value paradox: genome size against gene number
examples.description: 1,000 annotated reference genomes (NCBI Datasets) of bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants and animals. Genes scale with genome size in bacteria (b = 1.01, about 900 genes per Mb) but hardly in animals (b = 0.15) or plants (0.26): most of a big genome is not genes. Caveats: NCBI's first 200 per group, annotation-dependent counts.

examples.title: Caffeine in its receptor
examples.description: Caffeine bound in its real target, the human adenosine A2A receptor (RCSB 5MZP, 2.1 Å), in 3D, against adenosine, the agonist it blocks (2YDO). Contacts are computed from the coordinates: per residue within 5 Å, an H-bond candidate (N/O under 3.5 Å), π-stacking (ring centroids within 5.5 Å) or hydrophobic (C–C under 4 Å), with GPCRdb helix positions and UniProt binding sites. Idea: a molecule blocks a receptor by fitting its pocket without activating it: caffeine keeps adenosine's purine contacts (stacking on Phe168, an H-bond to Asn253) but, with no ribose, none of the ribose contacts (Ser277, His278) agonists use. Caveats: static snapshots of thermostabilised, mutated receptors (5MZP has Ala at 88 and 277); distance cutoffs, not energies or affinity; A1 is a caffeine target too.

examples.title: Can I fly ESSA → ESGG VFR now?
examples.description: A VFR go/no-go from every METAR and TAF in Sweden and its neighbours (NOAA AWC), SIGMETs and SMHI's model along the route: each TAF group graded against the SERA VMC minima (1500 ft, 5 km) in each airport's ±1 h window. The aha: the TEMPO/PROB groups, not the prevailing forecast or the METAR, decide a VFR flight a few hours out. Not an official briefing.

examples.title: Die yield: why big chips are expensive and chiplets exist
examples.description: Real die areas from Wikidata (Apple A-series to M1 Max, console APUs, GPUs, camera sensors) under Poisson, Murphy and negative-binomial yield models. Idea: yield falls exponentially with area, so a good mm² of a big die costs more, and splitting into tested chiplets recovers it. Caveats: defect densities and the chiplet overhead are scenarios; few die areas on Wikidata.

examples.title: Direct and indirect band gaps: why LEDs are not silicon
examples.description: Every stable element and binary compound with a gap in Alexandria (PBE) by family, from PubChem valences. Idea: an indirect gap needs a phonon to emit light; Si sits 1.9 eV above the direct line, GaAs, InP, GaN and Zn/Cd chalcogenides on it. Shares per family with Wilson intervals and a two-proportion test. Caveats: PBE gaps are 30–100% too small (Ge, InAs missing), small families.

examples.title: Moore's law and the end of Dennard scaling
examples.description: Fifty years of CPUs (Karl Rupp's trend data): transistors, clock, power, single-thread performance and cores on a log scale. Idea: a constant doubling time is a straight line in log2; the clock's best break year (2004) splits each trend, and a Chow test and Dennard's power budget (P ≈ N·C·V²·f) show transistors kept doubling every ~2 years while the clock and power went flat. Caveats: pre-2010 points digitised from a plot, high-end CPUs only, break chosen on the clock data.

examples.title: Why semiconductors are tetrahedral: the Mooser–Pearson map
examples.description: Octet AB compounds (Alexandria ground states, PubChem electronegativities) on Δχ against mean principal quantum number. Idea: covalent bonds between light atoms are tetrahedral (zincblende, wurtzite), ionic ones rock salt; one Δχ threshold sorts 87%, Fisher's line 91%. Caveats: Pauling Δχ is a crude ionicity; PBE puts Li halides in wurtzite.

examples.title: Vegard's law and lattice matching for epitaxy
examples.description: III-V binaries and ordered (In,Ga)As and (Al,Ga)As cells (Alexandria, PBE) with measured cells (COD). Idea: an alloy's lattice constant is linear in composition (Vegard), its gap bows; solving for InP gives In0.53Ga0.47As with measured cells (0.47 with PBE). Caveats: PBE lattice constants 1–2% large and gaps far too small; ordered, not random, alloys.

examples.title: Bragg's law and the selection rules of semiconductor crystals
examples.description: Simulated Cu Kα powder patterns of Si, Ge, diamond, GaAs, AlAs and InP from COD cell edges. Idea: Bragg's law plus the structure factor of a two-atom fcc basis: (200) is extinct in Si, faint in GaAs, strong in InP; a film's peak splitting grows as tan θ. Caveats: scattering factors approximated by Z, no thermal motion.

examples.title: Little's law in NumPy's CI
examples.description: Every GitHub Actions run of NumPy on one day, as intervals in Polars. Queueing idea: Little's law, L = λW: runs in flight minute by minute against arrival rate times mean duration, exact over the day, rough hour by hour, and split per workflow (L = Σ λᵢWᵢ), so the slow workflows hold the runners, not the frequent ones. Caveats: last update stands for the end; re-runs and late-updated runs excluded.

examples.title: Paintings
examples.description: Open-access (CC0) paintings from the Cleveland Museum of Art: an image grid, a table of who made them and when, and their creation dates on one time line. Statistics: a distribution and its quantiles, of dates that are ranges ("c. 1650" is 1645-1655): the median and the middle half are taken over each range's midpoint. Caveat: 24 paintings, one page (skip 120) of about 3,900 in the API's order, not a random sample of the collection; change skip or limit to see how stable the median is.

examples.title: CO₂ and income: elasticity
examples.description: CO₂ per person against GDP per person (PPP) for every country of a million people or more (World Bank), and six countries' paths since 1990. Statistics idea: an elasticity is a slope on log–log axes: across countries CO₂ rises about 1.1% per 1% of income, but within Sweden, the UK, Germany and the US it fell as they got richer: a slope between groups is not the relation within them, and neither is a cause. Caveats: territorial emissions, latest year per country.

examples.title: Codon usage bias: synonymous is not neutral
examples.description: 99 E. coli genes (Ensembl CDS, UniProt proteins): the genetic code read off the data, RSCU and Wright's Nc. Ribosomal proteins (median Nc 36.7) fall far below the mutation-only curve, regulators (51.3) stay near it: highly expressed genes use a preferred dialect of codons. Caveats: gene sets stand in for expression; short genes give noisy Nc.

examples.title: Copenhagen's wettest days
examples.description: Daily precipitation over Copenhagen 1940–2025 (Open-Meteo's ERA5 archive) and each year's wettest day. Statistics idea: extreme values: a Gumbel fit to the annual maxima gives return levels, the rain expected once in 10, 50 or 100 years on average, with 95% intervals, and the two halves of the record fitted apart. Caveats: a reanalysis grid cell smooths cloudbursts (2 July 2011), a 100-year level extrapolates, and the fit assumes a stable climate.

examples.title: Crypto markets
examples.description: CoinGecko's 20 largest coins by market cap: Polars turns the answer into rows and the 7-day hourly price sparkline into log returns, then a chart shows the day's moves, each coin's volatility against its week, and the correlation matrix of hourly returns (most coins move with Bitcoin). Prices are in US$; a week of hours is a small sample.

examples.title: CVE watch
examples.description: CISA's catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild: which vendors were added in the 90 days before the newest addition, which are used by ransomware, and each CVE with its required action and due date. A starting point for security and forensic triage. Statistics idea: waiting times. If additions came as a Poisson process, the days between addition days would be memoryless (geometric, the discrete exponential); CISA's working week and batch releases show up as departures from it. A vendor's count is not a rate: without its installed base (the exposure) it can't say whose products are riskier.

examples.title: Dinosaurs through time
examples.description: Every non-bird dinosaur genus in the Paleobiology Database: when each lived (first to last find), how many genera lived in each age of the Mesozoic and how fast they appeared and vanished, and where their fossils are dug up today against where those places were when the animals lived. Mind the third panel: the diversity curve rises and falls with how many fossils each age has. Next: The big five extinctions.

examples.title: Dragon-type Pokémon
examples.description: PokeAPI's Dragon type: every Dragon Pokémon's official artwork, which generation it came from, and the type chart: what Dragon hits hard and what hits it back. Statistics: a rate needs an exposure. Later generations look Dragon-heavy, but each brought a different number of new species, so the count is divided by that size and shown with a 95% interval (the generation sizes are the national Pokédex ranges, written into the step; alternate forms are left out). Next: the table's links lead to each Pokémon's own stats (base stats are a step away, one call per Pokémon).

examples.title: US drug recalls
examples.description: The 100 most recently reported drug recalls in openFDA's enforcement reports: which firms, how serious (Class I: may cause serious harm or death; II: temporary or reversible harm; III: unlikely to harm) and why. A count needs an exposure: all recalls per route of administration are divided by the products listed per route in the NDC directory, with a 95% Poisson interval, so a route with many products doesn't look riskier just for being big. A firm's count has no such denominator here. Reports are weekly; openFDA data are not for medical decisions.

examples.title: Earthquakes
examples.description: USGS's magnitude 4.5+ earthquakes of the past week, read from GeoJSON with Polars, ranked, and plotted on a world projection (hover a quake for its place, depth and time; click for its USGS event page). Statistics: the Gutenberg–Richter law, a power law: the number of quakes at least as strong as M falls about tenfold per magnitude, so on a log axis it is a straight line whose slope is the b-value (Aki's maximum-likelihood estimate, with its standard error). A week has only about a hundred M4.5+ quakes, so b is uncertain to about ±0.1; the catalogue mixes magnitude types (mb, Mww) and is complete only above about M4.5.

examples.title: Heart-rate variability from ECG beats
examples.description: Beat annotations of three Holter ECGs from PhysioNet (a healthy heart, MIT-BIH 100 and 119) turned into RR intervals and time-domain HRV (SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50) and Poincaré SD1/SD2. Ectopic beats and noise gaps fake variability: in record 119, 197 premature ventricular beats make RMSSD 437 ms from every beat against 36 ms from normal-to-normal intervals, and the PVCs show a full compensatory pause. Caveats: three people, 15-minute windows, no spectral HRV.

examples.title: The euro against seven currencies
examples.description: European Central Bank reference rates (via Frankfurter) since January 2025: each currency indexed to 100 at the start, so you can see which gained or lost against the euro, with the change, low and high per currency. Statistics: daily log returns (the change in the log of the rate, which add up over days) and their standard deviation, the volatility, per month and annualised (× √252), so a calm currency and a jumpy one can be told apart even when they end at the same place. ECB publishes once per working day around 16:00 CET; a month has only about 21 returns.

examples.title: EVs on the highway: regenerative braking and drag
examples.description: EPA city and highway energy per km for 5,000 vehicles: why EVs alone use more on the highway, and how drag grows with body size.

examples.title: Influenza's R: exponential growth, herd immunity and final size
examples.description: US flu seasons since 2016–17 (CDC FluView via Delphi), ILI+ on a log scale: exponential growth doubling in 8–20 days, so R is 1.1–1.3. The SIR model then gives a herd-immunity threshold near 13% and a final size near 26%. Caveats: ILI+ is a proxy; R depends on the generation interval; effective R, not R0. With a study plan.

examples.title: Gompertz's law: the risk of dying doubles about every seven years
examples.description: Eurostat life tables for eight countries, 2003 and 2023: from 35 to 84 the log death rate is a straight line, and the risk doubles every 6.6–10 years everywhere. Countries and decades differ in the level, not the rate of ageing (Strehler–Mildvan, r = −0.93). Off the line: the accident hump and the oldest ages.

examples.title: Grid frequency: the power balance meter
examples.description: One day of the European grid's frequency, every second (Energy-Charts, Freiburg). Control idea: frequency is the grid's balance meter, held by primary control acting as a proportional controller. Folded at the quarter-hour, a sawtooth appears: power is scheduled in 15-minute blocks, and a paired test over the 96 quarter-hours shows the jump when each one turns. Caveats: one day, one point; FCR power implied from the droop; inertia not in the data.

examples.title: The Gutenberg–Richter law and the b-value
examples.description: Every M ≥ 4.5 earthquake of 2025 (USGS): the frequency–magnitude distribution, completeness magnitude by maximum curvature, and the b-value by Aki–Utsu maximum likelihood (1.15 ± 0.02; near 1 for Mw alone). Ten times rarer per magnitude unit, yet the M 8.8 Kamchatka quake released about 83% of the year's energy. Caveats: mixed magnitude scales, no declustering.

examples.title: Hacker News
examples.description: What's on Hacker News' front page now, from the Algolia search API: points and comments per story (log scales, click a dot for the thread). Statistics idea: a heavy tail. A few stories hold most of the points, so the mean sits well above the median, the typical story; with 30 stories one hit moves the mean a lot.

examples.title: Hardy–Weinberg, and why pooled populations break it
examples.description: Genotypes of five famous variants (LCT, SLC24A5, ALDH2, ACTN3, HbS) in 26 populations of 1000 Genomes (Ensembl, IGSR). Each population sits on the p², 2pq, q² parabola; pooled, heterozygotes vanish by exactly F_ST (SLC24A5: F 0.67 against 0.65), the Wahlund effect. HbS in Africa has too many heterozygotes: selection. With a study plan.

examples.title: Heat pumps and the Carnot limit: why flow temperature matters
examples.description: A year of metered COP from four houses with the same heat pump (heatpumpmonitor.org) against the Carnot limit and the temperature lift.

examples.title: Public holidays this week
examples.description: Nager.Date's public holidays in every country it covers for the coming seven days, joined with country names: what is celebrated where, whether nationwide or regional. Statistics: Poisson counts. If holidays fell independently at a steady rate, the count per day would be Poisson around the week's mean; the dispersion index (variance over mean, 1 for Poisson) and P(at least this many) per day show whether they cluster instead. Caveat: one week is seven numbers, Nager.Date lists about 200 countries but how fully it records regional holidays varies, and a day with no holiday counts as zero.

examples.title: The hypsometric equation: why warm air stands tall
examples.description: Open-Meteo's temperatures and geopotential heights at 13 pressure levels in 17 columns from pole to pole along 20° E. Physics idea: the hypsometric equation Δz = (R/g) T̄ ln(p₁/p₂) reproduces the model's layer thicknesses to about 0.25%; warm columns are tall, the tropopause falls from 16.5 km to 8–11 km. Caveats: one moment's model state; dry air; below-ground levels excluded.

examples.title: The skip zone: why far stations hear you and near ones don't
examples.description: Live ionosonde readings (GIRO via KC2G): foF2, the secant law MUF = foF2·sec i, and the skip distance per amateur band.

examples.title: Iran: sites, airspace and odds
examples.description: Question: what is the state of the Iran conflict, and what do markets give for a nuclear deal, strikes, a leadership change or the Strait of Hormuz by a given month? The map lays Iran's nuclear and military sites (coordinates from Wikipedia, each linked), USGS's seismic events of the last 30 days (with the distance to the nearest site) and the aircraft OpenSky sees now on GMRT terrain: an empty Iran beside busy Gulf skies is what a closed airspace looks like. The odds chart is the ontology's 'outcome by deadline': each Polymarket 'by ...?' event is a probability curve over its deadlines (cumulative), and 'continues through ...?' a survival curve (the Israel-Iran ceasefire); Manifold adds play-money forecasts; UN News and GDELT the diplomacy. Caveats: there is no front line here, so 'who is winning' is read from the markets and the news, not from a map; nearly every seismic event in Iran is an earthquake (USGS labels an explosion only when it knows); OpenSky's receivers are sparse in the region, so an empty area can be missing coverage. Market prices are not probabilities (fees, thin trading; hollow dots break the ordering). GDELT allows one request every 5 seconds per address and may refuse: rerun it.

examples.title: How long issues stay open
examples.description: The 100 issues opened in the Polars repository in early March 2025 (GitHub search): closed, or still open. Statistics idea: survival analysis with censoring: an open issue lasted at least this long, and the Kaplan–Meier estimator with Greenwood's band gives the share still open after t days, for bugs and enhancements; its median is far above the median of the closed issues alone, which ignores the open ones. Caveats: one repository and two weeks; 'closed' includes 'not planned'.

examples.title: Kubernetes capacity and bin-packing
examples.description: Each node's allocatable CPU and memory against the requests of the pods on it: headroom, stranded resources, and how many more typical pods fit. Statistics: utilisation is a distribution over nodes, and free capacity only counts where a whole pod fits. Needs signing in and your cluster connected through your organization's gateway.

examples.title: Kubernetes warning events
examples.description: Your cluster's warning events over the last hour, by reason and object, and the ones that keep recurring. Statistics: events as a Poisson process, with a dispersion index and burst minutes (Bonferroni over the window). Needs signing in and your cluster connected through your organization's gateway.

examples.title: Kubernetes operations: evict a pod
examples.description: Pods that failed, are pending or keep restarting, the disruption budgets that protect workloads, and an eviction you run yourself: set namespace and pod, dry run, then evict. Changes your cluster; needs signing in, your organization's gateway and a token with a narrow Role.

examples.title: Kubernetes requests vs usage
examples.description: CPU and memory each container uses (metrics-server) against what it requests: over- and under-provisioned containers and idle requests per namespace. Statistics: a ratio on a log scale and its spread, median against pooled. Needs signing in, metrics-server, and your cluster connected through your organization's gateway.

examples.title: Kubernetes rollouts and image drift
examples.description: Deployments' desired, updated and available replicas, unfinished or stuck rollouts, pods still running an old image, and the versions of each image across deployments. Statistics: a version distribution, by its modal share and Simpson's diversity. Needs signing in and your cluster connected through your organization's gateway.

examples.title: Kubernetes workload health
examples.description: Your cluster's pods per namespace and phase, the containers that restart most and why, and those waiting in CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff. Statistics: restart counts are a heavy tail (the share restarted at least k times, log-log, against a thin-tailed count with the same mean). Needs signing in and your cluster connected through your organization's gateway.

examples.title: Kepler's third law in 5,600 exoplanets
examples.description: NASA Exoplanet Archive: period, semi-major axis and star mass of every planet. Physics idea: Kepler's third law P² = a³/M★; dividing by the star's mass collapses all orbits onto one line (slope 0.9985), and the star's mass can be read off any orbit. Forensic twist: about 55% agree to <1% because the archive computed a with the law itself. Caveats: composite rows mix references; planet mass neglected.

examples.title: Life expectancy around the world
examples.description: World Bank life expectancy at birth, each country's most recent year, joined in SQL with the World Bank's country list for region and income group (aggregates such as 'World' dropped) and with GDP per capita, with a summary per region. A least-squares regression of life expectancy on log GDP per capita shows how strongly the two go together, with a 95% band for the line, and which countries live longer or shorter than their income predicts; it is a correlation, not a cause.

examples.title: Sidebands in the power demand: the modulation theorem
examples.description: The Fourier spectrum of 8 weeks of German load: daily harmonics flanked by weekly sidebands at k ± j/7, windows, leakage and resolution.

examples.title: Mars in 3D: the spacecraft
examples.description: NASA's own 3D models of four Mars missions side by side: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Global Surveyor, the Opportunity rover and the Ingenuity helicopter. Switch between the scale their files have and the same size; hover one for what it did and its size in the file, click for NASA's file. Beside them, every Mars model science.nasa.gov lists, each a query away from 3D. Caveat: glTF's unit is the metre, but not every model keeps to it, so check a size against the mission's published one before comparing. Next: Perseverance: who built what, Mars rovers for their newest images, NASA in 3D for the whole catalog.

examples.title: Landing on Mars
examples.description: Every attempt to land on Mars, 1971–2021: where each one came down on NASA's map, how it went (10 of 16 worked), the landing system (parachutes and rockets, airbags, sky crane) and how long it lasted. Positions and stories are sourced per mission. Caveat: Mars 2's crash site is an estimate and Mars Polar Lander's is its target. Next: Mars rovers up close for the rovers to scale, Mars in 3D for NASA's models, Mars rovers for the newest images.

examples.title: Mars rovers
examples.description: Perseverance and Curiosity's newest raw images from NASA: the latest 24 of each as image grids, and of the newest 100 which cameras took them and on which sol (a Mars day). Statistics: a rate needs an exposure. The same 100 images can cover one sol or many, so images per sol divides by the sols the window spans, including sols with none, with a Poisson 95% interval; per sol with images it would be a different number. Caveats: the window is cut by count, so its first sol is partly missing and its newest sols are still being downlinked; images come in bursts (mosaics, drives), so the Poisson interval is too narrow.

examples.title: Mars rovers up close
examples.description: NASA's Mars rovers side by side and to scale in 3D: Sojourner (1997), Spirit and Opportunity (2004), Curiosity (2012) and Perseverance (2021). Hover a dot for a camera, instrument, solar panel, RTG, antenna or computer: what it does, its mass and power where a source states them, and a link to the source. Beside it, mass and power across the generations (a hundred times heavier, seven times the power) and where the watts go (MOXIE and Ingenuity drew more than the MMRTG makes). Caveats: shapes are simplified and positions approximate, not NASA's models; figures are from Wikipedia's rover and instrument pages; empty mass or power means no stated figure. Next: the raw images example shows what the cameras see today.

examples.title: Max-cut three ways
examples.description: Split a graph's nodes in two so that as many links as possible are cut: every split tried (exact), simulated annealing at nine schedule lengths, and how the same problem maps onto D-Wave's quantum annealer (an Ising model with J = +1 per link). How rare the best cut is, how often annealing finds it, and a study of whether slower schedules help. Caveat: at this size a laptop is exact; whether quantum annealing beats the best classical methods on large problems is open. Next: change the graph in the Graph step, or send it to D-Wave with your own Leap token (coming).

examples.title: The merit order: why sunny noons are cheap
examples.description: Germany's day-ahead price against load and residual load (Energy-Charts, May–June 2026): the empirical supply curve, the duck curve and which plants set the price.

examples.title: Molecules in 3D
examples.description: A small molecule from PubChem (caffeine; change the name in the query's path) as ball and stick from its computed 3D conformer, with its properties; and a protein from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (haemoglobin, 4HHB) as a backbone per chain with its haem groups. Statistics: the bond lengths, computed from the atoms' coordinates, form a distribution per bond kind: bands by kind, double bonds shorter than single ones, and the conjugated ring's C–N bonds spread between the two (a computed conformer with few bonds per kind, not a measurement). Hover atoms, bonds and chains; drag to orbit.

examples.title: Mushroom season in Sweden
examples.description: When do mushrooms fruit in Sweden? GBIF records per month (2000–2025) for the chanterelle, funnel chanterelle, porcini, fly agaric and false morel, against all fungi. Statistics idea: months are circular, so the season's centre is a circular mean (each month an angle on the year's clock) and its length R says how concentrated the season is; records follow effort (people search in autumn), so a second mean weights each month by the species' share over all fungi's share. Beside it, Mushroom Observer's 2025 chanterelle photos with the community's identification votes: in North America the 'chanterelle' is many species. Caveats: records are presence-only and follow observers; GBIF mixes citizen science and collections; Mushroom Observer is mostly North American. Next: hover the clock for dates, click an arrow for GBIF's map, swap a taxonKey (any species from GBIF's species search) or country.

examples.title: NASA in 3D: the model catalog
examples.description: Every 3D model science.nasa.gov publishes, read live from its WordPress media API: 358 glTF models and 7 STL files for printing, by collection (NASA 3D Resources, the solar system, Mars, missions), size and month added. Hover a dot for the model, click it for the file; Hubble opens in 3D below, and any model in the table opens the same way (a query of its url, viewModel in a graph). Awareness: the dates are when a file reached the rebuilt science.nasa.gov (the old NASA 3D Resources moved over in bulk in spring 2025), not when it was made; sizes run from kilobytes to almost 100 MB, and Seebra reads files up to 25 MB. Next: Mars in 3D, and Perseverance: who built what.

examples.title: Asteroids passing Earth this week
examples.description: NASA's NeoWs feed (JPL data) of near-Earth asteroids making their closest approach in the coming seven days: miss distance in lunar distances, estimated size and speed, and which are potentially hazardous (hover a dot for its record, click for its JPL page). Statistics: sizes span two orders of magnitude, so they are binned on a log scale, where the median and the geometric mean (the mean of the logs) describe a typical asteroid and the ordinary mean is pulled up by the few big ones. Sizes are modelled from brightness with an assumed albedo (min to max is a factor of about 2.2), small asteroids are only found when they pass close, and a week is a few dozen objects. Uses NASA's shared DEMO_KEY (30 requests an hour); put your own key in for more.

examples.title: Asteroids in 3D
examples.description: The asteroids passing Earth in the coming week (NASA NeoWs), around Earth in 3D: each at its real miss distance on a log scale with the Moon's orbit for reference, sized by estimated diameter, red when potentially hazardous (hover for the record, click for its JPL page). NeoWs gives no approach direction, so directions are illustrative. Statistics: the empirical cumulative distribution (ECDF) of miss distance on a log axis, so you can read off the median and the share within the Moon's distance, 10× and 100× it. A week is a few dozen objects, and the feed only lists approaches within about 0.5 au (195 lunar distances), so the curve reaching 100% there is the list's cut-off. DEMO_KEY allows 30 requests an hour. With the coming month's flybys as estimated trajectories past Earth (JPL's close approaches and orbits, two-body Kepler motion), checked against JPL's own distances.

examples.title: Fertiliser and diminishing returns
examples.description: Cereal yield against fertiliser use in 180 countries (World Bank/FAO): a Mitscherlich curve fitted in Polars by grid search shows each extra kilogram buying less grain: the first 50 kg/ha return about 41 kg of grain per kg, the next 200 about 10. Countries past the bend (China, Egypt, Viet Nam) gain little more, and countries' paths since 2000 show yields rising on less fertiliser.

examples.title: Nobel physics
examples.description: The Nobel Prize API's physics laureates, read as a table in Polars (one row per prize; John Bardeen has two), counted per decade and by country of birth. Statistics: a trend with an uncertainty band. The mean age at the award stayed near 50 until the 1960s and passed 70 in the 2020s; the band is the 95% interval of each decade's mean, and the ages' own spread is far wider. Caveats: age is award year minus birth year (within a year), a decade holds only 7 to 28 laureates (the 2020s are not over), and a rising age may reflect a longer wait between discovery and prize rather than older discoverers. Hover a dot for the laureate; click it for Wikipedia.

examples.title: Nordic GDP
examples.description: World Bank GDP per capita for the five Nordic countries since 2000, with yearly growth computed in Polars, and a principal component analysis (PCA) of the panel of yearly log growth: how much the five economies move as one, which years broke together, and which country goes its own way. Values are in current US$, so exchange rates are part of every move.

examples.title: Profile this page: where the main thread's time goes
examples.description: Seebra profiles itself: a Javascript Variable datasource reads window.__seebraPerf (long animation frames with their scripts and Seebra spans, board moves, interactions, fetches, LCP, resource timing), re-read every 15 s by a timer. Long frames are joined to the scripts in them and to board moves to say who spent the frame budget: Seebra, a third party, or a request during a pan. Chrome/Edge APIs; numbers depend on the machine.

examples.title: Perseverance: who built what
examples.description: NASA's own 3D model of the Perseverance rover, with Ingenuity beside it: hover a part (cameras, instruments, the arm and drill, the power source, antennas, wheels) and it lights up with what it does and which organizations designed, built or led it; click for the source. Beside it, every organization against the rover's systems, and the countries they're in. Perseverance is mostly JPL's, with instruments from France (SuperCam's mast unit), Spain (MEDA, the high-gain antenna), Norway (RIMFAX), Italy (LaRA) and Finland (MEDA's sensors), and companies from Austria to Japan. Caveats: only claims a fetched source states (JPL pages often name no outside builder, so a part with only JPL may have had others); a few countries are inferred (marked); dots mark parts the model has no shape for, at approximate positions; organization counts say nothing of money or effort. Next: Mars rovers up close compares four generations, and the raw images example shows what the cameras see.

examples.title: Central limit theorem: earthquake depths
examples.description: Depths of the past month's M2.5+ earthquakes (USGS): a strongly skewed population. Statistics idea: the central limit theorem: 500 random samples of 1, 5, 30 and 100 quakes, drawn in Polars, have means that approach the normal curve while their spread shrinks as σ/√n and their skewness as γ/√n. Caveats: the population is one month's feed, not all quakes, and aftershocks make quakes dependent; the resampled draws are independent.

examples.title: Response spectra: which buildings an earthquake shakes
examples.description: Ridgecrest M7.1 ShakeMap stations: SA(T)/PGA by distance, resonance and damping, and why distant quakes sway tall buildings.

examples.title: The Ramachandran plot: why proteins have helices and sheets
examples.description: Backbone angles φ and ψ of 606 residues of four proteins (PDBe validation, secondary structure). Half the residues lie in 1.4% of the plane: helices and strands are two sterically allowed basins, positive φ is glycine's, proline's φ is pinned. Caveats: four proteins; approximate region boxes.

examples.title: Cross-correlation: a dam's pulse down the Grand Canyon
examples.description: Two weeks of 15-minute discharge at Lees Ferry and near Grand Canyon (USGS). Signals idea: time-delay estimation by cross-correlation, as in GPS and radar: Glen Canyon Dam's daily pulse takes about 21 h to cover 141 km (about 6.6 km/h), but a peak a day later is almost as high: a periodic signal fixes a delay only modulo its period. Caveats: tributaries, celerity is not water speed.

examples.title: River rating curve: the Missouri at Hermann
examples.description: How a river gage turns water level into discharge: a power law Q = C (h − e)^b fitted in Polars to 4,117 USGS field measurements since 1928. Per decade, the stage that carries 40,000 ft³/s fell from 7.1 to 3.4 ft as the bed cut down (one all-years curve under-reports today's low flows by ~44%), and at flood stage the same level has carried 418,000 to 750,000 ft³/s: the 100-year flood sits where the curve is weakest.

examples.title: Upcoming rocket launches
examples.description: The next 30 orbital launches from The Space Devs' Launch Library 2: when (and how sure the date is), who, which rocket and pad, and what they carry (hover a launch for its record, click for its Launch Library page). Statistics: Poisson waiting times. If launches came at random at a steady rate, the gaps between them would be exponential, a straight line on a log axis; the last 100 launches are compared with that model, with the rate per day and the chance of a day without a launch. The ratio sd / mean of the gaps is 1 for a Poisson process (below: more regular, above: clustered by campaigns, ranges and weather); the 100 launches give only 99 gaps, and they are past launches because upcoming dates known only to the month pile up at its end. The free API allows 15 requests an hour (this dashboard makes two).

examples.title: The most-edited science fiction
examples.description: Open Library's science-fiction subject: the 48 works with the most editions, their covers, when they first appeared and how often they were reprinted, and which decades they come from. Statistics: a rate needs an exposure, and the sample is selected on the outcome. Ranked by editions, old works win because they have had longer to collect reprints; editions per year in print (counted to 2026) reorders the list. A few works carry no usable first-publication year (Open Library records 0); they stay in the table but are left out of the charts. Edition counts include translations and reprints that Open Library merged into one work, so they are a rough measure.

examples.title: Service status
examples.description: Live status of the services a platform team depends on (GitHub, Cloudflare), from their public Statuspage summaries: every component with its status, and how many are not operational per service. Cloudflare lists hundreds of components (one per data centre), GitHub a dozen, so compare shares, not counts.

examples.title: The ground is a low-pass filter
examples.description: Three years of hourly air and soil temperature at four depths under Berlin (Open-Meteo, ERA5-Land). Systems idea: the frequency response of a diffusive system: each cycle is damped as e^(−z/d) and delayed by z/d with d = √(2κ/ω). Fourier harmonics in SQL give the daily and annual damping depths, κ, and their ratio against √365; the lag passes 90°, impossible for one RC stage. Caveat: reanalysis soil, thick layers.

examples.title: The solar cycle, found by a periodogram
examples.description: The monthly sunspot number since 1749 (SILSO v2 via NOAA SWPC). Signal idea: a periodogram computed in SQL finds the 11-year Schwabe cycle; cycle minima from a windowed minimum give 25 cycles of 9–13.6 years; flipping every other cycle's sign moves the peak to 22 years, the magnetic Hale cycle. Caveats: sparse early data; the flip assumes strict alternation.

examples.title: The solar system to scale
examples.description: The Sun to Jupiter with every distance to scale: each planet where JPL's Keplerian elements put it today, wearing NASA's textures (NASA's Sun, Mercury and Venus models, NASA 3D Resources' Earth, Mars and Jupiter), and 3,000 numbered asteroids plus the Jupiter trojans from JPL's Small-Body Database, each on its own orbit. Run time forward a month a second; hover a planet for its orbit and distance, an asteroid for its name and group. Beside it the Kirkwood gaps: asteroids by orbit size, with Jupiter's resonances (3:1, 5:2, 7:3, 2:1) emptying their distances and gathering the Hildas (3:2) and the trojans. Awareness: planets are drawn 1000 times and the Sun 20 times their size, or they would not show (True sizes); the elements are JPL's approximation for 1800-2050 (arcminutes for the inner planets); numbered asteroids are the first found, so biased to the large and bright. Next: NASA in 3D, Mars in 3D.

examples.title: Hot Python questions on Stack Overflow
examples.description: The 50 'hot' Python questions on Stack Overflow from the Stack Exchange API: views against age, whether they have an answer yet, and which other tags travel with Python right now (exploded and counted in Polars). Statistics idea: correlation is not causation. Spearman rank correlations of score, answers, views and age show what rises together, but age drives all of them, and the 'hot' list was chosen on those same numbers, so the sample is selected on the outcome (50 questions). Without a key the API allows 300 requests a day per IP.

examples.title: Star Wars bodies and the square-cube law
examples.description: SWAPI's 82 characters: mass grows as height^1.54 ± 0.12, flatter than the BMI's 2 and far from the square-cube law's 3, so tall aliens are lanky and small ones dense (costumes and CGI, not biology). Jabba weighs 19× a Star Wars body of his height; starship cost grows as length^1.4. Fan-made data from Lucasfilm's films.

examples.title: Stefan–Boltzmann on the HR diagram
examples.description: 3,000 random Gaia DR3 stars with good parallaxes: luminosity from brightness and distance, radius from L = 4πR²σT⁴, on an HR diagram with lines of equal radius. At the same temperature, giants are 10× larger and 100× brighter than dwarfs; L ∝ M^4.7 on the main sequence. Checked against Gaia's FLAME and GSP-Phot. Caveats: Malmquist bias, model masses, BC_G valid 3,300–8,000 K.

examples.title: Stockholm weather
examples.description: Open-Meteo's hourly forecast for Stockholm, summed per day, and each day's mean temperature as an anomaly against the 1991–2020 normal for that calendar day from Open-Meteo's ERA5 archive: a z-score, the difference in standard deviations of that day's 30 years. Forecast (modelled) against reanalysis (modelled from observations); 30 values per calendar day make the spread itself uncertain.

examples.title: Sweden's electricity today
examples.description: Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE, from ENTSO-E data) public net generation in Sweden today, every 15 minutes: nuclear, hydro, wind, solar and the rest stacked against the load, with net exports, and each source's mean and peak output. Statistics: correlation is not causation. The correlation matrix of the sources over today's quarter hours shows what moves together; hydro follows the load because operators steer it, while other pairs only share the clock. One day of quarter hours, each close to the last, is far less evidence than the count of rows suggests.

examples.title: Temperature across Sweden now
examples.description: SMHI's latest hourly air temperature from every reporting weather station in Sweden, on a map from Smygehuk to Abisko, with the warmest and coldest stations. Statistics: a straight-line trend of temperature against latitude, with a 95% band for the line (and a wider one for a single station), so you can see how much colder each degree north is this hour and how sure that slope is. One hour is a snapshot; height and coast also matter. Quality G is checked, Y is suspect or not yet checked.

examples.title: Swedish wildlife
examples.description: Recent photographed sightings in Sweden from GBIF (many from iNaturalist): the photos as a grid, which classes of life they show and who took them. Statistics: a count of sightings is not abundance, it follows observer effort. Bird records per province are divided by all photographed records there (the exposure) into a share with a 95% interval; the big provinces lead in counts, not in share. Caveats: a share is still not abundance, and GBIF's province names mix counties and historical provinces.

examples.title: Aliasing: a fake two-week tide
examples.description: Four months of hourly water levels at San Francisco (NOAA), read every 1, 6, 11, 24 and 25 hours, with a Fourier transform of each in SQL. Signals idea: Nyquist–Shannon and aliasing: read once a day, the 12.42-hour tide becomes a fake 14.7-day wave as large as the real one, exactly where alias theory puts it; daily means (a low-pass filter) remove it. Caveat: the alias period happens to be close to the real spring–neap cycle.

examples.title: Trouton's rule: the vapour pressure from the boiling point
examples.description: Wikidata vapour pressures and boiling points for 326 pure liquids: Clausius–Clapeyron with Trouton's constant entropy of vaporisation predicts most vapour pressures within a factor of 2 from the boiling point alone; hydrogen-bonded liquids (alcohols, glycols, acids) evaporate about half as readily as predicted.

examples.title: Ukraine: front, forces and odds
examples.description: Question: who is gaining ground in Ukraine, where are the forces, and what do markets give for a ceasefire, a peace deal or territorial concessions by a given month? The map lays DeepStateMap's areas of control (now, and the line of 1 January 2026 dashed) on GMRT terrain, with its attack directions, the Russian units and airfields it places, and 120 days of its located updates (each a place it reports changing hands). The area step measures the net change in km² since 1 January; the weekly chart counts reported advances by side. The odds chart is the ontology's 'outcome by deadline': each Polymarket 'by ...?' event is a probability curve over its deadlines (a cumulative distribution), so you can read the chance of a ceasefire before a month and year; Manifold adds play-money forecasts; UN News and GDELT the diplomacy. Caveats: DeepStateMap is a Ukrainian volunteer project (sources: its own, the General Staff, geolocated footage); its unit positions are its placements, not verified here, and a quiet sector is unreported rather than unchanged. Market prices are not probabilities (fees, thin trading; hollow dots break the ordering). GDELT allows one request every 5 seconds per address and may refuse: rerun it. Terrain is about 7 km per cell.

examples.title: Uppsala since 1840: when warming leaves the noise
examples.description: Uppsala's daily minimum temperature since 1840, read as one CSV straight from NOAA's public GHCN-Daily S3 bucket. Every season warmed about 3 °C against 1850–1900, but signal-to-noise is 1.4 in winter and 3.5 in summer: 28 of the last 30 summers were warmer than any pre-industrial one, against 14 of 30 winters (time of emergence). The frost-free season grew from 118 to 151 days. Caveats: not homogenised, urban heat island, gaps.

examples.title: Wikipedia top
examples.description: English Wikipedia's most-viewed articles on 1 November 2026 from the Wikimedia pageviews API, without the main page and special, project and talk pages (click a bar or dot to read the article). Statistics idea: Zipf's law. On log-log axes views against rank fall close to a straight line, a power law views ≈ C · rank^(−s); the fit gives s. Caveats: the API lists only the top 1000, views include some automated traffic, and news spikes bend the head of the curve.

examples.title: Wind power: the cube law and the Betz limit
examples.description: Westermost Rough's metered output (Elexon) against ERA5 wind: the power curve, P ∝ v³, Cp against Betz's 16/27.

examples.title: Your own data
examples.description: Where to get your own data out of 22 common platforms (Spotify, Google Timeline, Apple Health, Strava, Netflix, your bank and more), which file in each export matters, and what to look at. Two worked examples run on made-up samples shaped like the real files: Spotify's listening history and Netflix's viewing history. Drop your own export on the board and point the transformation at it.
